obtained.how: the GSA meeting-abstract page (the abstract is the whole publication), served by GSA's Confex/m-anage program site

bibliography.note: Blair-Glantz, S., Wilson, K. & Willis, T. V. 2009. Zooplankton population analysis and body length measurement in Damariscotta Lake, Maine in relation to alewife populations. GSA Abstracts with Programs 41(3): 111; Northeastern Section 44th Annual Meeting (22–24 March 2009), Session 55, Paper No. 3 (poster). University of Southern Maine. The entry agrees. It is a conference abstract, so the paper's '(abstract only)' is accurate as a description of the publication type.

claims.claim: in Damariscotta Lake daphniids "dropped sharply after juvenile alewives appeared" (quoted)
claims.source_value: the abstract's words are 'their populations dropped dramatically soon after the appearance of alewife juveniles' (of Daphniidae, 'initially abundant')
claims.quote: their populations dropped dramatically soon after the appearance of alewife juveniles
claims.conditions: Damariscotta Lake, Maine; 5 monthly samples June–October 2008; eight zooplankton groups counted and measured; two basins (zooplankton more abundant and larger in the main north basin than the Muscongus south basin)
claims.note: The meaning is right but the words in quotation marks are not the source's: quote it exactly or paraphrase without quotation marks. The alewife link is the authors' interpretation: the abstract reports no alewife sampling and says the changes 'correspond to the time of the summer that juvenile alewives would be expected to' eat larger zooplankton; it also offers basin morphology or productivity as explanations for the basin difference.

notes: Other points in the abstract: average Daphniidae body length 'dropped somewhat' over the five months; copepod nauplii increased greatly in number and slightly in size. No numbers (densities or lengths) are given.
